title: Setup: your machine, your tools, your public record
hook: Six months from now the proof of what you can do is a public record: a repository of programs, write-ups and a lab you built. Week one builds the tools that record it - and the habit of closing every step on evidence.

read.title: Read: GitHub docs - about GitHub and Git (the vocabulary you will use every day)

gift.for: your future self and every recruiter who looks
gift.what: A public GitHub repository under your own name with a README that states the six-month plan and its gates - the first thing in the record.

taught: how this programme works (evidence closes a step; the 1/7/30/90-day review; the logbook); PowerShell basics (pwd, ls/Get-ChildItem, cd, mkdir, cat/Get-Content, tab completion, Ctrl+C); winget installs; python --version / git --version / code --version; Git: init, status, add, commit, log, remote, push; GitHub repository, README, .gitignore; gh auth login; TryHackMe account and the in-browser AttackBox; how to read official documentation (python docs, man pages at man7.org, an RFC's sections)

steps.title: How this school works - and why every step closes on evidence
objectives: State the three rules: one idea per step, a step closes on evidence in your own words, passed skills return on the 1/7/30/90-day ladder
Say what the six-month gate is and which phase you are in
steps.tutor_brief: FIRST STEP OF THE PROGRAMME. WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: today you learn how the school itself works; because the method is the product - 520 hours spent without a closing rule produce tabs, not skills; for every step after this. ONE IDEA: a step closes when the one thing its objectives name has been done or said - a program printed the right thing, a command's output was pasted, an idea was explained in his words - never because time passed. Explain the practice spine in two lines: every skill a checkpoint passes comes back in the warm-up after 1, 7, 30 and 90 days; a miss pulls it back sooner. Explain the logbook: each step ends with his 'I CAN NOW' sentence plus the evidence; that log is exported to his repo monthly. State the six-month gate plainly (Security+ passed; 60+ programs public; a hardened Linux lab; networking at Network+ level; applied cryptography demonstrated; 30+ rooms and 20+ write-ups; the finance strand incl. a tokenization brief; 5+ job applications) and that he is in Phase 0 (setup, week 1) of six phases. Ask ONE question that proves he has the closing rule: 'what closes a step - and what never does?' EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: his sentence names evidence (not time, not message count). Then the usual close.

steps.title: PowerShell: the terminal you already have
objectives: Open Windows Terminal/PowerShell and navigate with pwd, ls, cd, mkdir; read a file with cat; use Tab completion and Ctrl+C
Create the folder tree C:\Users\<you>\sec-lab with notes/ and code/ inside, from the terminal only
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: the terminal, because every tool in security is a command first and a window second; for every day from now on. ONE IDEA: a shell is a program that takes a command line, runs it and prints what came back - the prompt shows where you are. MANUAL (numbered): 1) Win+X -> Terminal (or search 'PowerShell'); 2) `pwd` (Get-Location) - read the path; 3) `ls` - read the listing; 4) `mkdir sec-lab`, `cd sec-lab`, `mkdir notes, code`; 5) `echo "day 1" > notes\log.txt` then `cat notes\log.txt`; 6) type `cd se` and press Tab - completion; 7) run `ping 127.0.0.1 -t` and stop it with Ctrl+C. Each step: what he should see. Teach that PowerShell aliases ls/cat/pwd onto Get-ChildItem/Get-Content/Get-Location - the Linux names will carry over to Bandit and the VM. He pastes the output of `ls` inside sec-lab showing notes and code. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the pasted listing + his one-line explanation of what a shell is. Boundary Question: what happens if he runs `cd` to a folder that does not exist - have him try and read the error.

steps.title: Install the toolchain: Python, Git, VS Code (winget)
objectives: Install Python 3.12+, Git for Windows and VS Code with winget; prove each with its --version
Open the sec-lab folder in VS Code from the terminal with `code .`
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: the three tools of the whole programme; because installing from a package manager (not a browser download) is the professional habit and reproducible; for every code step. ONE IDEA: a package manager installs, upgrades and removes software from a trusted catalogue by name. ALREADY DONE? first: `python --version`, `git --version`, `code --version` - anything that answers is installed. MANUAL: 1) `winget install -e --id Python.Python.3.12`; 2) `winget install -e --id Git.Git`; 3) `winget install -e --id Microsoft.VisualStudioCode`; 4) close and reopen the terminal (PATH is read at start); 5) the three --version commands; 6) `cd ~\sec-lab` then `code .`; 7) in VS Code: Extensions -> install 'Python' (Microsoft). If winget is missing (older Windows 10): App Installer from the Microsoft Store, then retry. If `python` opens the Store: Settings -> Apps -> App execution aliases -> turn off python.exe aliases. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the three version strings pasted. He states in one line why a package manager beats a browser download (one trusted source, upgrades, scriptable). SECRETS: no account is needed for any of this; if any installer asks to sign in, skip it.

steps.title: Git: a history you can trust
objectives: Explain what a commit is (a snapshot with a message and a parent) and why a history matters
Run git init, status, add, commit and log in sec-lab, with your name and email set

links.label: Pro Git, ch. 1.3 - What is Git?

steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: Git, because every program and write-up for six months goes into a history you can show and roll back; for the portfolio and for every job. ONE IDEA: a commit is a snapshot of the folder plus a message plus a pointer to the previous snapshot - the chain is the history. Draw it (three boxes, arrows back). MANUAL: 1) `git config --global user.name "<his real name>"` and `user.email` (the address he will use on GitHub); 2) `git config --global init.defaultBranch main`; 3) in sec-lab: `git init`; 4) `git status` - read 'untracked'; 5) `git add notes/log.txt`; 6) `git commit -m "Day 1: lab folder and first note"`; 7) `git log --oneline`. Then: change log.txt, `git status` (modified), `git diff`, add, commit again, `git log --oneline` shows two lines. Vocabulary he must say back: working tree, staging area (index), commit. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: `git log --oneline` with two commits pasted and his one-line definition of a commit. Boundary Question: what does `git add .` stage that he might not want (secrets, big files) - this is why .gitignore exists (next step).

steps.title: GitHub: the public record begins
objectives: Create a public repository under your own name, push sec-lab to it with gh, and add a README that states the six-month plan
Explain the difference between Git (local) and GitHub (a remote host), and what a .gitignore is for
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: GitHub, because the record only counts if others can see it; for every recruiter and for his own 'did I really do this'. ONE IDEA: Git is the history on his disk; GitHub is a copy of that history on a server (a remote) that others can read. SECRETS LAW: authentication happens in the browser via `gh auth login` - he never pastes a token or password into this chat, and no token goes into a file in the repo. MANUAL: 1) `winget install -e --id GitHub.cli`; reopen terminal; 2) `gh auth login` -> GitHub.com -> HTTPS -> Login with a web browser - follow the code in the browser (he does this himself); 3) in sec-lab create `.gitignore` with `__pycache__/`, `.venv/`, `*.log`, `.env` - say why each; 4) write README.md: his name, 'Six months: cybersecurity, Python, cryptography, digital finance - Dec 2026 to May 2027', the eight gates as a checklist; 5) `git add .`, commit 'README: the plan'; 6) `gh repo create sec-lab --public --source=. --remote=origin --push`; 7) open the repo URL and read it. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the repository URL (public) and his one line on Git vs GitHub. If he already has a GitHub account under a handle, the repo still goes under his real-name account - this record is professional.

steps.title: TryHackMe: your sanctioned target range
objectives: Create a free TryHackMe account, start the in-browser AttackBox and complete the 'Linux Fundamentals Part 1' room
State the sanctioned-targets rule and the two Criminal Code sections that make it law in Canada

links.label: TryHackMe - sign up (free tier is enough for the first weeks)
Criminal Code s. 342.1 - unauthorized use of computer

steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: TryHackMe, because hands-on practice needs a target that invites it, and the in-browser AttackBox gives him a Linux machine today with nothing installed on this PC; for every room and CTF until May. ONE IDEA: the sanctioned-targets rule - you touch only your own machines, your lab, and systems that explicitly invite testing; anything else is s. 342.1 (unauthorized use of a computer) and s. 430(1.1) (mischief to data) of the Criminal Code of Canada. Say it once, plainly, not as a lecture. MONEY: the free plan is enough now; if the site offers a paid plan, he picks free - no price, no card, is needed for this step (costs money only later, by his own decision outside the programme). MANUAL: 1) sign up (email + a password he creates in his own password manager - never typed here); 2) open the room, 'Start AttackBox' (browser machine); 3) work through tasks 1-8 - the commands (echo, whoami, ls, cd, cat, pwd, find, grep) are the ones he met in PowerShell; 4) answer the room's questions in the room, not here; 5) when complete, paste the room's completion line and his TryHackMe profile URL. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the profile URL showing the room completed + the rule in his words. Add the profile link to README (one commit).

steps.title: Reading the source: docs, man pages, RFCs
objectives: Find the answer to three questions in official documentation alone (python docs, man7.org, an RFC) and cite the section
Explain the structure of an RFC (status, abstract, sections, MUST/SHOULD language) and why primary sources beat blog posts
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: reading primary sources; because an expert is someone who reads the manual before the forum, and in security the standard IS the answer; for every later step where you point him to the docs instead of explaining. ONE IDEA: official documentation is organised, versioned and exact - learn its shape once and you can answer your own questions. Three finds, one per message, he answers with the citation: (a) in the Python docs: what does `str.strip()` remove when called with no argument? (library/stdtypes); (b) at man7.org: in `man ls`, which option sorts by modification time? (-t); (c) in RFC 2119: the exact difference between MUST and SHOULD. Teach the RFC skeleton: header/status, abstract, table of contents, numbered sections, security considerations, references. He says why a primary source beats a blog (exact, current, authoritative, the thing itself). EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: three correct answers with their sources named. This step has no code.

Teach it back
steps.prompt: Explain to a new colleague, in writing, how your working record is built: what a commit is, where the history lives, what GitHub adds, what .gitignore keeps out, and what the closing rule of this programme is. Use your own repo as the example. 6-10 sentences, exact vocabulary.

title: Investment Funds in Canada (IFC): the whole exam, chapter by chapter
hook: You have the textbook and a date to beat. This module is not a lecture - it is the exam turned into recall: eighteen chapters pulled into twelve passes, each one closed only when you can say the idea back and work its numbers. The exam is 100 questions, 60% to pass, and it rewards KYC, fund structure, fund evaluation and regulation above all - so that is where the weight of this module sits.

read.title: Read: CSI - the official IFC curriculum (the 18 chapters, in CSI's own words; your textbook is the primary source)

gift.for: your exam and the job after it
gift.what: ifc/ - a KYC and suitability one-pager, a registered-plans comparison table (RRSP/RRIF/TFSA/RESP/RPP), a formulas sheet (total return, NAVPS, MER drag, bond price-yield direction, quartiles) and a mock-exam log - the sheet you revise from the morning of the exam and keep for the client-facing job.

taught: the IFC exam shape (1 proctored exam, 100 MCQ, 3 hours, 60% pass, 85% Honours, 3 attempts) and the official topic weightings; Ch1-2 the representative's role and the Canadian financial marketplace (capital, instruments, markets, intermediaries, securities regulation); Ch3 economics (business cycle, interest rates, money and inflation, fiscal/monetary/international policy); Ch4-5 the KYC communication process, the financial-planning process, the life-cycle hypothesis, and behavioural biases applied to asset allocation (the highest-weight topic); Ch6 the Canadian tax system and registered plans; Ch7 investment products and how they trade (fixed income, equities, bond pricing, new issues, derivatives); Ch8-9 constructing portfolios (risk/return, calculations, management) and reading financial statements; Ch10 the modern mutual fund (what it is, how organized, how regulated - NAVPS); Ch11-13 fund product types (conservative, riskier, alternative managed - ETFs, seg funds, hedge funds, PPNs); Ch14-15 fund performance and selection (quartiles, comparison universes, volatility's effect); Ch16 fees and services (MER, sales charges, SWPs, taxation of distributions); Ch17 dealer regulation (CIRO, registration, KYC rules, account opening, prohibited practices); Ch18 ethics and standards of conduct; the house rule: suitability is a professional skill for a client, never personal advice to you

steps.title: Ch 1-2: the representative's role and the Canadian marketplace
objectives: Explain the mutual fund representative's role and the licensing/registration that permits it, and define KYC and suitability at the level Ch1 introduces them
Name the parts of the Canadian financial marketplace: investment capital, the main instruments, primary vs secondary markets, the intermediaries, and who regulates securities
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: the opening block (weighting 'Introduction to the Mutual Funds Marketplace' ~13%); because the exam opens here and because the rest of the course hangs off two ideas introduced now - the representative acts in the client's interest (suitability), and a fund trades inside a regulated marketplace; for every later chapter. ONE IDEA PER PASS: (a) the representative is a registered, licensed salesperson whose core duty is suitability - matching a recommendation to a known client; (b) the marketplace moves capital from savers to users through instruments (debt, equity, managed products) in primary (new issue) and secondary (resale) markets, via intermediaries (dealers, banks, exchanges), under securities regulation that is provincial. He has the textbook open; this is recall, not first contact. He states each in his own words and answers three self-quiz questions he picks from the chapter. HOUSE RULE, once: suitability is how he will advise a CLIENT; it is not advice to him about his own money. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: role + KYC/suitability defined, the marketplace parts named, three chapter questions right. Boundary Question: primary vs secondary market - in which does the issuer receive the money (primary) - a favourite exam distinction.

steps.title: Ch 3: economics - the cycle, rates, money, policy
objectives: Describe the business cycle's phases and the main indicators (GDP, employment, inflation/CPI) and state how interest rates relate to bond prices and to economic activity
Distinguish fiscal from monetary policy and name the Bank of Canada's role
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: economics as context; because suitability and fund selection both depend on where the cycle and rates are, and the exam tests the mechanisms, not predictions; for Ch7 (bond pricing) and Ch8 (portfolios). ONE IDEA: the economy moves in a cycle (expansion, peak, contraction, trough); rates are the price of money - the Bank of Canada sets the policy rate (monetary policy), governments tax and spend (fiscal policy), and bond prices move opposite to rates. Recall drill: he places two indicators in the cycle and states the rate-bond inverse in one line with a reason (a fixed coupon is worth less when new bonds pay more). He picks three self-quiz questions. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: cycle phases + indicators named, the rate/bond-price inverse explained with its reason, three questions right. Boundary Question: inflation rises and the Bank raises the policy rate - what happens to the price of a bond fund he already holds, and why (down; existing coupons less attractive) - tested often.

steps.title: Ch 4-5: Know Your Client and behavioural finance (the heaviest topic)
objectives: Walk the KYC communication process end to end (gather, clarify, confirm) and the financial-planning process, and link the life-cycle hypothesis to changing objectives and risk capacity
Name four behavioural biases (e.g. overconfidence, loss aversion, anchoring, hindsight) and say how each would distort an asset allocation
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: KYC and behaviour; this is the single HIGHEST-WEIGHT exam topic (the KYC communication process ~19%) so it gets the most of his attention here; for the account-opening and suitability rules in Ch17. ONE IDEA: suitability is built from KNOWING the client - objectives (what for), time horizon, risk tolerance AND risk capacity, and personal/financial circumstances - gathered through a structured communication process and kept current; behavioural biases are the predictable ways clients (and he) misjudge risk, which the process exists to counter. Recall: he runs the KYC process in his own words against a made-up client HE invents (never real advice), and maps two biases to a wrong allocation they would cause. He picks four self-quiz questions (this topic earns four, not three - it is 19% of the exam). EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the KYC process and planning process in order, life-cycle link made, four biases with their allocation effect, four questions right. Boundary Question: risk TOLERANCE vs risk CAPACITY - a client comfortable with risk but near retirement - which one limits the recommendation (capacity) - the exam's favourite trap.

steps.title: Ch 6: tax and retirement planning - the registered plans
objectives: Explain the structure of the Canadian income-tax system at the level Ch6 needs (marginal rates, types of income: interest, dividends with the gross-up/credit idea, capital gains inclusion) and why tax treatment differs by income type
Compare RRSP, RRIF, TFSA, RESP and RPP on contribution, growth and withdrawal, and compute a simple RRSP tax-deferral benefit
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: tax and registered plans; because tax treatment drives real suitability and is heavily examinable, and the registered-plan table is pure memorisation he must own; for Ch16 (fund taxation). ONE IDEA: income is taxed by TYPE (interest fully taxed; eligible dividends grossed-up then a credit; only part of a capital gain is included) and registered plans change WHEN and WHETHER growth is taxed. He builds the comparison table into ifc/ (RRSP: deductible in, taxed out; TFSA: not deductible in, tax-free out; RRIF: the RRSP's payout phase with a minimum; RESP: grants, taxed in the student's hands; RPP: employer pension). Numeric: a $5,000 RRSP contribution at a 30% marginal rate defers $1,500 of tax now - he works it and states what is taxed later. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the income-type treatment in his words, the completed plan table committed to ifc/, the deferral number right. Boundary Question: interest vs eligible-dividend income of the same dollar amount - which is taxed more heavily, and why that steers fund-type suitability (interest; it is fully included).

steps.title: Ch 7: investment products and how they trade
objectives: Describe fixed-income securities (coupon, maturity, par, the price-yield inverse) and equities (common vs preferred, dividends, voting), and state what a new issue (primary) is versus secondary trading
Explain in one line each what a derivative is and the two basic kinds (options, forwards/futures) as the funds will use them
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: the underlying products; because a mutual fund is a basket of exactly these, and Ch11-13 name the funds by what they hold; for fund types and for FIN1/FIN2 overlap. ONE IDEA: a fund owns securities - debt (lends at a coupon, price moves opposite to yield), equity (owns a share, variable dividend, last in line), and sometimes derivatives (a contract whose value derives from something else, used to hedge or gain exposure). Recall: he classifies five instruments and restates the bond price-yield inverse with a reason (met in Ch3 - now with the instrument in hand). He picks three questions. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: fixed income and equity features named, primary vs secondary stated, derivative defined, three questions right. Boundary Question: a preferred share vs a bond of the same issuer - which ranks ahead in a wind-up and which has a fixed maturity (bond both) - a classic compare.

steps.title: Ch 8-9: building portfolios and reading financial statements
objectives: Define risk and return, compute a total return (including distributions) and read standard deviation as a risk measure, and state what diversification does and does not remove
Name the three main financial statements and what each tells you about a company a fund might hold
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: portfolio and statement basics; because fund evaluation (Ch14-15) and suitability both rest on risk/return arithmetic, and the exam asks you to compute a return; for Ch14. ONE IDEA: return is what you earned (price change PLUS distributions, over what you put in); risk is the variability of that return (standard deviation), and diversification cuts the risk unique to one holding but not market-wide risk. Numeric he works: bought at $10, now $11, paid $0.40 in distributions -> total return = (11 - 10 + 0.40)/10 = 14%. Statements: balance sheet (what it owns/owes), income statement (what it earned), cash flow (where cash moved). He picks three questions. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the 14% worked correctly, risk/diversification stated, the three statements named with their purpose, three questions right. Boundary Question: two funds, same average return, different standard deviation - which is 'better' and for whom (lower SD for lower risk capacity) - links straight back to Ch5.

steps.title: Ch 10: the modern mutual fund - structure, organization, regulation
objectives: Explain what a mutual fund is (an open-end pool, units issued and redeemed at NAVPS), how it is organized (manager, custodian, trustee, distributor) and compute NAVPS
State how funds are regulated and what the Fund Facts document is for
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: the product itself; because everything before this was the ingredients and everything after is varieties and evaluation of THIS; for Ch11-16. ONE IDEA: a mutual fund is an open-end pool - you buy and sell UNITS directly with the fund at the net asset value per unit, priced once a day; separate parties manage, hold (custodian) and oversee it, and it is regulated (National Instrument rules; Fund Facts delivered to the buyer). Numeric: assets $10,500,000, liabilities $500,000, units 1,000,000 -> NAVPS = (10,500,000 - 500,000)/1,000,000 = $10.00. He explains why an open-end fund's unit count changes daily (new money/redemptions) unlike a stock. He picks three questions. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: fund defined, the four roles named, NAVPS computed, Fund Facts purpose stated, three questions right. Boundary Question: a closed-end fund and an ETF trade on an exchange at a price that can differ from NAVPS - why an open-end mutual fund cannot (it transacts AT NAVPS) - sets up Ch13.

steps.title: Ch 11-13: the fund product types, conservative to alternative
objectives: Sort the main fund types by risk: money market and mortgage and bond funds (conservative); equity, balanced, global and specialty (riskier); and name what each holds
Explain the alternative managed products - PPNs, hedge funds, closed-end funds, ETFs, segregated funds - and the one feature that defines each
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: the product map; because matching a fund TYPE to a client is the exam's applied core, and seg funds and ETFs carry distinct exam points; for selection (Ch14-15) and suitability. ONE IDEA: fund types are a risk ladder defined by what they hold - cash-like (money market) up to concentrated equity (specialty); the 'alternative' products each add one twist (PPN: principal guarantee at maturity; hedge fund: wide mandate, limited access; closed-end: fixed units, exchange-traded; ETF: index-like, exchange-traded, low cost; segregated fund: an insurance contract with maturity/death guarantees and potential creditor protection). Recall: he places six funds on the risk ladder and states each alternative product's defining feature. He picks four questions (three chapters). EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the ladder ordered, holdings named, five alternatives each pinned to their feature, four questions right. Boundary Question: a segregated fund vs a mutual fund holding the same stocks - what does the insurance wrapper add and cost (guarantees + possible creditor protection; higher fees) - a reliable exam item.

steps.title: Ch 14-15: measuring and selecting a fund
objectives: Explain performance measurement: time periods, comparison universes, benchmarks and quartile ranking, and why past performance is not a promise
Walk the selection steps and state how volatility affects realised returns (why a smoother path can beat a higher-average, choppier one)
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: evaluation; because 'fund evaluation' is a named high-focus exam area and it is where Ch8's risk/return becomes a decision; for the job. ONE IDEA: you judge a fund against the RIGHT peers and benchmark over sensible periods - a first-quartile fund is in the top 25% of its universe - and you weigh consistency, not just the headline number, because volatility drags compound returns. Recall: he ranks a fund given its quartile, lists the selection steps in order, and explains in one line why -50% then +50% does not get you back to even (the volatility drag met in FIN2, if he has done it; here from Ch15). He picks three questions. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: quartiles and universes explained, selection steps ordered, the volatility-drag point made, three questions right. Boundary Question: a fund top-quartile over 1 year but third-quartile over 10 - which matters more for a long-horizon client and why (the longer, consistent record) - judgement, the exam's favourite.

steps.title: Ch 16: fees, services and the taxation of fund returns
objectives: Name the fee types (management fee and MER, sales charges: front-end, deferred/DSC legacy, no-load, trailing commissions) and compute the drag an MER puts on a gross return
Explain accumulation plans and systematic withdrawal plans, and how fund distributions (interest, dividends, capital gains) are taxed in a non-registered account
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: fees and tax; because fees are the most consequential controllable in a fund and the exam tests MER arithmetic and distribution taxation, and client-focused reforms pushed fee transparency; for suitability and the job. ONE IDEA: the MER is the annual cost expressed as a percent of assets and it comes straight off the return every year; a fund's distributions keep their tax character (interest, dividend, capital gain) and are taxed in the client's hands unless sheltered. Numeric: 6% gross return, 2% MER -> ~4% net; over years that gap compounds (he states the direction and why). He explains a SWP in one line (regular redemptions for income) and the tax of a capital-gains distribution (partial inclusion, from Ch6). He commits the MER-drag line to ifc/. He picks three questions. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: fee types named, the 6% -> 4% worked, distribution taxation stated, three questions right. Boundary Question: the same fund in a TFSA vs a non-registered account - where do the distributions escape tax, and how that changes suitability (TFSA) - ties Ch6 and Ch16.

steps.title: Ch 17: dealer regulation - CIRO, registration, KYC rules, account opening
objectives: Name the current regulators and self-regulatory structure (CIRO since 2023, the provincial regulators under the CSA, and the investor protection fund), and the registration a representative needs
List the account-opening and KYC regulatory requirements, prohibited selling practices, and the representative's legal responsibilities
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: regulation; part of the 'Ethics, Compliance and Mutual Fund Regulation' ~16% bucket and the most date-sensitive chapter - make sure the textbook's regulator names are current (CIRO replaced the MFDA/IIROC in 2023); for the job and for staying on the right side of the rules he learned in SETUP1. ONE IDEA: a representative works for a registered dealer, is registered in the province, must complete KYC and keep it updated, must open and document accounts to rule, and is barred from specific practices (unsuitable recommendations, unauthorised trading, misrepresentation, borrowing from clients). Recall: he names the regulator map (CSA = the provincial regulators; CIRO = the SRO for dealers and marketplaces; the MFDA Investor Protection Corporation now under CIRO) and lists four prohibited practices. FLAG: if his textbook (he enrolled Sept 2026) still says MFDA, he notes the CIRO update - a live-fact check, two sources, exactly the SETUP1 habit. He picks four questions (16% bucket, shared with Ch18). EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the regulator map current and in his words, account-opening/KYC rules listed, four prohibited practices named, four questions right. Boundary Question: an unauthorised trade vs an unsuitable trade - the difference and why both are prohibited (consent vs fit) - a compliance staple.

links.label: CIRO - the current self-regulatory organisation (confirm the regulator names against your textbook)

steps.title: Ch 18: ethics and standards of conduct
objectives: State the standards of conduct (priority of client interest, integrity, competence, confidentiality, compliance) and apply them to two case scenarios from the chapter
Explain why ethics is tested separately from regulation - the difference between what is legal and what is right
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: ethics; the capstone of the 'Ethics, Compliance and Regulation' ~16% bucket and, not by accident, the same builder-defender spine as the rest of his programme - the rules bind the person, not the paperwork; for the exam's scenario questions and for the job. ONE IDEA: the standards put the client's interest first and hold the representative to integrity, competence, confidentiality and compliance; a scenario question asks you to pick the response that honours those even when a shortcut is legal. Recall: he reasons through two case scenarios aloud (he invents or uses the chapter's), naming which standard each tests. He picks three questions. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the standards named, two scenarios reasoned to the right action with the standard named, three questions right. Boundary Question: an action that is legal but breaches a standard of conduct (e.g. a suitable-but-self-serving recommendation) - why the standard still governs - the exam's ethical core, and his programme's.

steps.title: IFC mock checkpoint (weighted like the real exam)
Teach it back
steps.prompt: Write ifc/README.md as if briefing a new bank hire who must pass IFC next month: the exam shape (questions, time, pass mark, attempts) and the three highest-weight topics; how the KYC process builds suitability and why risk capacity can override risk tolerance; the registered plans in one line each; what a mutual fund is and how NAVPS is priced; the fund risk ladder and what seg funds and ETFs add; how MER and distribution taxation eat returns; and who regulates the dealer today (CIRO). 18-22 sentences, exact vocabulary. title: Python I: the machine does exactly what you say
hook: Every security tool you will ever use is a program; every analyst who gets promoted can write one. Two weeks from now you write programs that decide, repeat, store and check - and you can predict what they print before you run them.

ONE IDEA: a string is a sequence - index from 0, slice [a:b] stops before b, methods return a NEW string (strings do not change in place). steps.title: Decisions - if, elif, else, and the booleans behind them
objectives: Predict and write if/elif/else chains with and/or/not; explain short-circuiting
Write a function-free port classifier that says well-known / registered / dynamic / invalid
steps.starter:
# PY1-C4: predict first.
port = 8080
if port < 0 or port > 65535:
    print("invalid")
elif port < 1024:
    print("well-known")
elif port < 49152:
    print("registered")
else:
    print("dynamic")

attempts = 6
locked = attempts >= 5 and not False
print(locked)

# Your turn: set port to 443, 70000, 60000 - predict each, run each. Then: why is the  < 0 or > 65535  test FIRST?
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: decisions; because every rule in a firewall, a SIEM alert and a trading limit is an if; for everything. ONE IDEA: a chain of if/elif/else runs exactly one branch - the first true test wins - so ORDER is logic. Predict: registered; True. Three reruns: well-known, invalid, dynamic. The question 'why is the invalid test first' is the lesson: if it came last, 70000 would print dynamic - validation before classification, always (this is input validation, the first defensive habit). Teach and/or/not and that `a and b` stops at a if a is False. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: three correct predictions and his reason for the order in one sentence. Boundary Question: port = "443" (a string) - what breaks and where.

steps.title: Repetition - for, range and the accumulator
objectives: Predict for loops over range(a, b, step) and trace an accumulator pass by pass
Count failed logins per rerun of a loop and print a total
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: loops; because scanning 65,535 ports or 10,000 log lines is one loop; for the scanner and the parser. ONE IDEA: a for loop runs its block once per item; an accumulator is a variable updated on every pass. He traces the third loop in a table BEFORE running (1->1, 2->3, 3->6, 4->10). range stops before the end value: `range(20, 26, 2)` gives 20, 22, 24 - he predicts it. Your-turn: `for n in range(2, 101, 2)`; 2550. If he writes range(2, 100, 2) he gets 2450 - the off-by-one lesson; have him explain the fix. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: his program prints 2550 and he states the stop-before rule. Boundary Question: range(5, 1) - how many passes? Zero - try it.

steps.title: while, break, continue - loops that do not know when they end
objectives: Predict while loops; say when one stops and what an infinite loop looks like
Write a retry loop that stops after 3 failures or on success
steps.starter:
# PY1-C6: predict first.
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print("count", count)
    count = count - 1
print("done")

tries = 0
guess = "wrong"
while tries < 3:
    tries = tries + 1
    if guess == "secret":
        print("in after", tries)
        break
    print("try", tries, "failed")
print("locked out" if tries == 3 and guess != "secret" else "ok")

# Your turn: delete the line  count = count - 1  in the first loop, predict, run, read the 'ran too long' line, put it back.
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: while; because a server waits for connections, a brute-force tool retries, a monitor loops until stopped - and account lockout is exactly this loop; for sockets in PY2/NET. ONE IDEA: while re-asks its question before every pass and stops the first time it is False; break leaves early. Predict both blocks (count 3,2,1, done; try 1/2/3 failed, locked out). The deleted-line experiment: the editor stops a program after 10 seconds and says it ran too long - he reads that line; that is an infinite loop, and the missing update is the bug. Then he sets guess = "secret" and predicts 'in after 1'. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: both predictions right (or corrected with reason) and the infinite-loop line read and fixed. Boundary Question: a lockout counter that is never reset - what does that do to a legitimate user (denial of service by design).

steps.title: Double-entry: the invariant that makes ledgers trustworthy

Explain why an invariant is a security property (what an attacker would have to break)
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: double-entry; because every ledger he will build or audit - bank, blockchain, trading book - lives or dies on one invariant: debits equal credits, total balances sum to what was issued; for ledger.py next step and for blockchain state in FIN4. ONE IDEA: every transaction changes at least two accounts by equal and opposite amounts, so the totals never drift - an inconsistency is always detectable. Four worked rows on a T-account table, he fills the last two. Then the security framing: an invariant is a property that must hold after every operation; fraud or a bug shows up as a violation, so the ledger is audit-ready by construction - this is why we will write `assert balanced()` after each posting. steps.title: Build: a double-entry ledger that cannot go out of balance
objectives: Implement accounts as a dict and postings as a list; post a transfer and assert the invariant
Make the ledger reject a posting that would overdraw an account, and explain the difference between invalid and unbalanced
steps.starter:
# FIN1-C1: a tiny double-entry ledger. Every posting moves amount from one account to another.
accounts = {"abid": 100, "friend": 0, "bank_fees": 0}
entries = []

def balanced(issued):
    return sum(accounts.values()) == issued

def post(src, dst, amount, memo):
    if amount <= 0:
        return "rejected: amount must be positive"
    if accounts[src] < amount:
        return "rejected: insufficient funds"
    accounts[src] -= amount
    accounts[dst] += amount
    entries.append((src, dst, amount, memo))
    return "ok"

print(post("abid", "friend", 40, "e-transfer"))
print(post("abid", "bank_fees", 1.5, "fee"))
print(post("friend", "abid", 500, "too much"))
print(accounts, balanced(100))
# Your turn: 1) add a posting to an account that does not exist - which error? Add a check that rejects it.
# 2) Boundary Question: post("abid", "abid", 10, "self") - is the ledger still balanced? Is it a valid transfer? Decide and enforce.
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: the ledger in code; because the invariant becomes real when the program checks it, and this is the data structure under every payment system and every blockchain state; for FIN4 (where the 'accounts' are addresses) and the record. ONE IDEA: invariants are checked in code after every mutation. Predict the four prints (ok; ok; rejected: insufficient funds; the dict with 58.5/40/1.5 and True). Task 1: KeyError -> add `if src not in accounts or dst not in accounts: return "rejected: unknown account"` - validate BEFORE mutating (order again). Task 2: a self-transfer keeps the invariant but is meaningless - he decides (reject) and says why 'balanced' is not the same as 'valid'. Floats: 58.5 is fine here; say once that real money uses integers of cents or Decimal, never float - and let him convert the ledger to cents as an optional extra. HIS MACHINE: save as sec-lab/fin1/ledger.py, commit 'fin1: double-entry ledger with invariant', push. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the output pasted, both tasks enforced, the commit.

steps.title: Clearing, settlement, finality - and why timing is risk
objectives: Define clearing, settlement and finality and place them on a timeline for a card payment and an e-Transfer
Explain gross vs net settlement and the trade-off (liquidity vs credit risk); define RTGS
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: the three words; because 'instant' payments are usually instant messaging with settlement later, and every fintech and token claim is a claim about finality; for the Canadian rails next and for FIN4/FIN5. ONE IDEA: clearing = exchanging and reconciling the instructions; settlement = the actual transfer of the asset (central-bank money between banks); finality = the point after which it cannot be reversed. Timeline on a card payment: authorization (seconds), clearing (that night), settlement (T+1/T+2), chargeback window (months) - so a merchant's 'approved' is not final. Gross settlement: each payment settled one by one in full (needs liquidity, no credit exposure); net: obligations netted over a period (saves liquidity, builds exposure until settlement - Herstatt risk, name it once). RTGS = real-time gross settlement = Lynx in Canada. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: his timeline with the three words placed and his one-line trade-off. Boundary Question: what happens to a net system if one bank fails at 15:00 before the 17:00 settlement.

# PY2-C4 ON YOUR MACHINE: sec-lab/py2/authparse.py. Run: python authparse.py sample_auth.log --top 3
import argparse, sys
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

def parse_line(line):
    # 'Nov 19 03:14:07 lab sshd[812]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9 port 51022 ssh2'
    if "Failed password for" not in line:
        return None
    words = line.split()
    try:
        ip = words[words.index("from") + 1]
        user = words[words.index("for") + 1]
        if user == "invalid":
            user = words[words.index("user") + 1]
    except (ValueError, IndexError):
        return None
    return user, ip

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Top attacking IPs from an SSH auth log")
    ap.add_argument("log")
    ap.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=5)
    args = ap.parse_args()
    path = Path(args.log)
    if not path.exists():
        print(f"error: no such file: {path}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
    ips = Counter()
    users = Counter()
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
        for line in f:
            parsed = parse_line(line)
            if parsed:
                users[parsed[0]] += 1
                ips[parsed[1]] += 1
    for ip, n in ips.most_common(args.top):
        print(f"{ip:16} {n}")
    print("users tried:", dict(users.most_common(3)))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

steps.starter:
# PY2-C6 ON YOUR MACHINE: sec-lab/py2/fim.py
# Usage:  python fim.py baseline <folder> <baseline.json>      python fim.py check <folder> <baseline.json>
import argparse, json, hashlib, sys
from pathlib import Path

def file_sha256(path):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for block in iter(lambda: f.read(1 << 20), b""):
            h.update(block)
    return h.hexdigest()

def snapshot(folder):
    root = Path(folder)
    return {str(p.relative_to(root)): file_sha256(p) for p in root.rglob("*") if p.is_file()}

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="File-integrity monitor v1")
    ap.add_argument("mode", choices=["baseline", "check"])
    ap.add_argument("folder")
    ap.add_argument("baseline")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    now = snapshot(a.folder)
    if a.mode == "baseline":
        Path(a.baseline).write_text(json.dumps(now, indent=2))
        print(f"baseline: {len(now)} files")
        return
    old = json.loads(Path(a.baseline).read_text())
    added = sorted(set(now) - set(old))
    removed = sorted(set(old) - set(now))
    modified = sorted(k for k in now.keys() & old.keys() if now[k] != old[k])
    for label, items in (("ADDED", added), ("REMOVED", removed), ("MODIFIED", modified)):
        for k in items:
            print(label, k)
    sys.exit(1 if (added or removed or modified) else 0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: a real defensive tool; because tamper detection on system files is a control in every framework (PCI DSS req. 11.5 names FIM), and this is the whole idea of Tripwire/AIDE/Wazuh's syscheck in 40 lines; for the Security+ phase (he installs Wazuh and recognises it) and the record. title: Flipper Zero I: the device, the law, and the subsystems you own
hook: A Flipper Zero is not magic - it is a small microcontroller wired to a handful of radios and ports, each one a real protocol you can learn. Owning it 'in every aspect' means owning those protocols: what each subsystem actually does, why some of the systems it touches are weak, and the one rule that separates a security learner from a crime. This part builds the foundation and the parts you can master today on your own hardware.

read.title: Read: Flipper Zero official documentation (the primary source for every subsystem - you will return to it all the way through)

gift.what: flipper/ - a lab notebook (README) that names every subsystem and the protocol under it, the firmware you run and why, and the sanctioned-targets rule in your own words; plus an infrared universal remote and a UART read of your own Arduino, both documented. The first evidence that you treat the device as an engineer, not a button.

taught: what a Flipper Zero is (an STM32 microcontroller + sub-GHz CC1101 radio, 125 kHz RFID, 13.56 MHz NFC, infrared, iButton/1-Wire, GPIO, USB) and which real protocol each subsystem speaks; the menu map and the SD card layout; charging, updating and the qFlipper / mobile app; official vs custom firmware (Unleashed, Momentum, RogueMaster) and the legal line a custom firmware can cross (region/TX-power unlocks); the sanctioned-targets rule and Canada's Criminal Code s. 342.1 (unauthorised use of a computer) and s. 430(1.1) (mischief to data), plus the Radiocommunication Act point that transmitting on and jamming licensed bands is a separate offence; infrared as a protocol (carrier frequency + encoded bursts, NEC/RC-5), learning and replaying your OWN appliances, building a universal remote; GPIO and serial: the pinout, UART (TX/RX/GND, baud, async framing), reading your OWN Arduino's serial output with the Flipper as a USB-UART bridge; how to read a signal/protocol entry in the docs before you touch a button

steps.title: What a Flipper Zero actually is - one microcontroller, several radios
objectives: Name each subsystem (sub-GHz, 125 kHz RFID, 13.56 MHz NFC, infrared, iButton/1-Wire, GPIO, USB) and the real protocol or band it works with
Charge it, update to the latest official firmware with qFlipper or the mobile app, and navigate the menu to each subsystem
steps.tutor_brief: FIRST FLIPPER STEP. WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: what the device is, because 'mastering a tool' starts with knowing it is not one tool but seven small ones bolted to a microcontroller, and every later step is one subsystem; for all of FLIP1 and FLIP2. ONE IDEA: the Flipper is an STM32 microcontroller (the brain, like the Arduino's chip he will meet in HW1) connected to separate radios and ports - sub-GHz (a CC1101 transceiver, ~300-928 MHz regional bands, the stuff of simple remotes), 125 kHz RFID (low-frequency access fobs), 13.56 MHz NFC (contactless cards), infrared (TV/AC remotes), iButton/1-Wire (contact keys), GPIO (18 pins to wire to other hardware), and USB. Each is a real protocol he will learn one at a time - today is the map, not the attack. MANUAL: 1) charge it; 2) install qFlipper on the PC (winget: `winget install -e --id Flipper.qFlipper`) OR the mobile app, connect, and run the official firmware update - read what the updater says it is doing; 3) walk the top menu and find each subsystem; 4) note the SD card holds the apps and saved files. SECRETS/ACCOUNTS: no account is needed to use the device; if the mobile app offers one, it is optional - skip it; never type a password here. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: he lists the seven subsystems with the band/protocol of each, in his own words, and states the firmware version now on the device. Boundary Question: which subsystems only RECEIVE/read by default and which can TRANSMIT - and why that distinction is the whole legal question (next step).

steps.title: The one rule: sanctioned targets, and the law that makes it law
objectives: State the sanctioned-targets rule and apply it to five situations (your own car fob, a friend's car with their written OK, a hotel key, a stranger's card on a train, your own Arduino)
Name Canada's Criminal Code s. 342.1 and s. 430(1.1) and the Radiocommunication Act transmit/jamming point, and say which subsystem actions are reception (passive) vs transmission (regulated)
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: the rule, because a Flipper makes a line that is normally abstract (unauthorised access) one button-press wide, and crossing it is a crime in Canada regardless of intent or curiosity; for every hands-on step for the rest of his life. He already met this in SETUP1-L6 - here it is specific to a radio device. ONE IDEA: you may read, capture, analyse and transmit ONLY against your own devices, your own lab, and systems whose owner has explicitly invited testing. Everything else is off-limits. Say the law once, plainly, not as a sermon: s. 342.1 (unauthorised use of a computer) and s. 430(1.1) (mischief in relation to data) of the Criminal Code of Canada cover using the device against systems that are not yours; separately, the Radiocommunication Act makes transmitting on licensed bands and jamming a distinct federal offence - jamming is never a learning exercise. Reception/analysis of your own signals is how you learn; transmission is where law and physics both bite. Five situations he classifies out loud (his own fob: yes; friend's car: only with their clear OK and ideally in writing; hotel/work key: no - not his system; stranger on a train: no, and it is the textbook offence; his own Arduino over GPIO: yes). CONNECT TO DEFENCE: the reason to learn each attack is to specify the defence - that is the builder-defender frame of the whole programme. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the rule in his words, the two Criminal Code sections named, and the five situations correctly sorted into owned/sanctioned vs off-limits with a one-line reason each. Boundary Question: a YouTube video shows cloning a car key in 20 seconds - name two reasons it is both a crime and, on any modern car, a demo that does not work (rolling codes - FLIP2) - scepticism plus the law.

links.label: Criminal Code s. 342.1 - unauthorised use of a computer

steps.title: Firmware literacy: official vs custom, and the line a firmware can cross
objectives: Explain what firmware is, the difference between official firmware and custom firmware (Unleashed, Momentum, RogueMaster), and exactly what a custom firmware changes
State why a region/TX-power unlock can turn a legal device into an illegal transmitter, and decide which firmware you will run and why
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: firmware literacy, because the single most consequential choice he makes with the device is which software runs on it, and the forums push custom firmware without saying what it unlocks; for every transmit-capable step in FLIP2 and for staying legal. ONE IDEA: firmware is the program that runs on the microcontroller; the hardware is identical, the firmware decides what it is allowed to do. Official firmware ships with region limits and a conservative feature set - it respects, for example, the sub-GHz frequencies and power your region permits. Custom firmwares (Unleashed, Momentum, RogueMaster) add convenience, extra apps and - the part that matters - can remove region and transmit-power restrictions and enable transmitting on bands his region does not allow. Removing that limit does not change the law; it just makes the device capable of breaking it. He reads one custom-firmware changelog/readme as a primary source and identifies which changes are cosmetic, which are genuinely useful (UI, app loading), and which touch transmission limits. DECISION he must make and justify: for a learner on owned/sanctioned targets, official firmware is the honest default; if he ever runs a custom firmware he keeps region limits on and knows exactly what he changed. SECRETS/MONEY: firmware is free; never buy a 'pre-loaded' device or a paid firmware - it is the free one repackaged. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: firmware defined in his words, the three custom firmwares named with what they change, the legal line stated, and his own firmware decision with a reason. Boundary Question: 'the firmware made it legal because the menu let me' - why the menu is not the law (the Radiocommunication Act binds the person, not the UI).

steps.title: Infrared: your first subsystem, mastered on your own appliances
objectives: Explain infrared as a protocol (a modulated carrier ~38 kHz plus an encoded burst pattern; NEC and RC-5 as examples) and why it is line-of-sight and short-range
Learn the signals from your OWN TV/AC/soundbar remotes into the Flipper and build a single universal remote that controls them
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: infrared, because it is the one subsystem with essentially no legal hazard (your own appliances, no regulated band, no access control) so it is where he learns the whole workflow - read a protocol entry, capture a signal, save it, replay it, organise a library - with the stakes at zero; for the method that every later subsystem reuses. ONE IDEA: an IR remote blinks an LED at a carrier frequency (often 38 kHz) and encodes a button as a pattern of on/off bursts in a named protocol (NEC, RC-5, Sony SIRC); the Flipper has a wide-band IR receiver and a strong emitter, so it can learn a button and reproduce it. MANUAL (his own gear only): 1) read the Flipper docs IR page; 2) Infrared -> Learn New Remote, point his TV remote at the Flipper, press one button, name and save it; 3) repeat for a few buttons; 4) test that the Flipper now controls his TV; 5) try the 'Universal Remote' and note how it brute-forces common codes (fine on his own TV); 6) build one saved remote that holds his TV + AC + soundbar. He explains why pointing it at a neighbour's window does nothing useful and why IR does not pass through walls (line-of-sight) - the physics bounds the risk. HIS MACHINE/RECORD: export the saved .ir file, add it and a short note to flipper/ in sec-lab, commit 'flip1: IR universal remote for my own appliances'. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the Flipper controls at least two of his own appliances, he names the protocol one of them used, and the commit exists. Boundary Question: an IR signal he cannot learn in one try - what to check (angle, distance, battery, a protocol the receiver did not decode) - debugging a capture, the skill that carries to every radio.

steps.title: GPIO and UART: wire the Flipper to your own Arduino and read it talk
objectives: Explain the GPIO header and UART (TX/RX/GND, baud rate, asynchronous framing of start/data/stop bits) and why TX connects to RX
Use the Flipper's USB-UART bridge (or GPIO UART) to read the serial output of your OWN Arduino sketch, and capture a few lines
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: GPIO/UART, because the deepest 'hacking tool' use of a Flipper is the most benign - it is a hardware lab instrument that talks to other chips, and reading a device's serial lines is the first move in real hardware security; for HW1 (his Arduino kit) and for FLIP2's hardware ideas. ONE IDEA: UART is two wires carrying asynchronous serial - one side's TX (transmit) goes to the other side's RX (receive), a shared GND reference, and both must agree a baud rate (e.g. 9600 or 115200); a byte is framed by a start bit, 8 data bits and a stop bit. Prerequisite: this is best done when his Arduino kit is unboxed (HW1, ~20 Dec) - if it is still boxed, he does the reading/explanation now and the wiring when it is open. MANUAL (his own boards): 1) read the GPIO pinout page, find GND and the UART pins (13/TX, 14/RX); 2) flash a trivial Arduino sketch that does Serial.begin(9600) and Serial.println a counter; 3) wire Arduino TX -> Flipper RX, Arduino RX -> Flipper TX, GND -> GND (cross TX/RX - say why: one talks, the other listens); 4) on the Flipper use GPIO -> USB-UART bridge (or a UART terminal app) at 9600; 5) read the counter lines; 6) capture a few lines to the SD/notebook. SAFETY (hardware, not legal): match voltage (both 3.3 V logic here), never wire power rails together blindly, GND first. RECORD: a note + the captured lines in flipper/, commit 'flip1: read my Arduino over UART with the Flipper'. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the captured serial lines pasted, and his explanation of why TX goes to RX and what baud means. Boundary Question: wrong baud rate - what the output looks like (garbage/garbled bytes) and why (the receiver samples at the wrong rate) - the single most common serial bug.

End with the one sentence you would want a new owner to read first.

title: Markets and trading mechanics: how a price is made (paper only)
hook: A tokenized bond, a crypto exchange and the TSX all do one thing: match buyers and sellers and settle the result. Before you can read a DeFi protocol or a market-structure rule you must know the order book cold - and you will build one.

read.title: Read: CIRO - for investors (who regulates Canadian dealers and marketplaces, and what they publish)

steps.title: What a market is, and the three kinds
objectives: Define a market by venue, instrument and participants; distinguish exchange, OTC and dealer markets with a Canadian example of each
State the house rule of the finance strand and why a mechanism course gives no advice
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: markets as systems; because tokenization is 'put this instrument on this ledger and let it trade' - the instrument and the trading are the old part; for every FIN step after this. ONE IDEA: a market is a mechanism that turns intentions to buy and sell into a price and a transfer; the mechanism differs by venue type. Exchange (central order book, anonymous, standardised: TSX equities), OTC (bilateral, negotiated: most bonds, FX, swaps), dealer/quote-driven (a dealer quotes two-way prices: Canadian bond dealers, a crypto 'instant buy' is a dealer trade with a hidden spread - name it). Say the house rule plainly once: this strand teaches how it works, never what to buy; every trade in the programme is paper; his real money is outside the programme. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the three kinds with correct Canadian examples and the rule in his words. Boundary Question: in which of the three does the customer not see the other side's price (dealer) - and what does that mean for the spread he pays.

steps.title: The limit order book: bids, asks, spread, depth
objectives: Read a level-2 order book, name best bid/offer, spread and depth, and predict what a market order of a given size executes at
Explain why the spread exists and who earns it
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: the order book; because it is the data structure of every exchange including crypto venues, and matching is what he builds next step; for FIN4/FIN6 (AMMs are the alternative to a book - he must know what they replace). ONE IDEA: resting limit orders sit in two sorted queues; a market order walks the opposite queue, best price first, until filled - so size moves price (slippage). Draw a 5-level book (bids 100.10x300, 100.05x500, ...; asks 100.20x200, 100.25x400, ...). He reads: best bid 100.10, best ask 100.20, spread 0.10, then computes the average fill of a 500-share market buy (200 @100.20 + 300 @100.25 = 100.23). The spread: compensation to liquidity providers for adverse selection and inventory risk - two sentences, no more. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the fill arithmetic right and his one line on the spread. Boundary Question: a market order in a thin book at 03:00 - what is the worst fill; why limit orders are the default for anyone who is not a market maker.

steps.title: Order types and what each one risks
objectives: For market, limit, stop, stop-limit, IOC, FOK, day and GTC orders: say what triggers, what executes, and the failure mode
Explain a stop order's gap risk and a stop-limit's non-execution risk with one numeric example each
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: order types; because every trading interface and every exchange API (including crypto) exposes them, and most retail losses are an order type misunderstood; for the engine (which will support market and limit) and the journal. ONE IDEA: an order is a conditional instruction - the condition (trigger) and the execution rule (price limit, time in force) are separate. Table he completes: market (now, any price - slippage); limit (at my price or better - may never fill); stop (becomes a market order when price touches X - gaps: stop at 95 fills at 80 on a gap-down); stop-limit (becomes a limit at Y when X touches - may not fill in a crash, you keep the position); IOC/FOK (partial or all-or-nothing immediacy); day/GTC (time in force). Two numeric examples he works. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the completed table and the two examples. Boundary Question: an exchange API with a bug that treats a limit price as a quantity (it has happened) - what protects you (client-side validation, max order size) - defence in trading systems is input validation again.

steps.title: Build: a price-time-priority matching engine
objectives: Implement an order book with two sorted queues, limit and market orders, partial fills and a trade log; keep the invariant that no bid rests at or above a resting ask
Write five tests (assert statements) that document the rules, and commit
steps.starter:
# FIN2-C4: a tiny matching engine. Prices in integer cents - never floats for money.
# Orders: dict(id, side 'buy'|'sell', price (None for market), qty). Book: bids sorted high->low then time; asks low->high then time.
bids, asks, trades = [], [], []
_seq = 0

def place(side, qty, price=None):
    global _seq
    _seq += 1
    order = {"id": _seq, "side": side, "price": price, "qty": qty}
    book = asks if side == "buy" else bids
    while order["qty"] > 0 and book:
        best = book[0]
        crosses = price is None or (side == "buy" and best["price"] <= price) or (side == "sell" and best["price"] >= price)
        if not crosses:
            break
        fill = min(order["qty"], best["qty"])
        trades.append({"price": best["price"], "qty": fill, "taker": order["id"], "maker": best["id"]})
        order["qty"] -= fill
        best["qty"] -= fill
        if best["qty"] == 0:
            book.pop(0)
    if order["qty"] > 0 and price is not None:
        rest = bids if side == "buy" else asks
        rest.append(order)
        rest.sort(key=lambda o: (-o["price"] if side == "buy" else o["price"], o["id"]))
    return order

def best_bid(): return bids[0]["price"] if bids else None
def best_ask(): return asks[0]["price"] if asks else None
def invariant(): return best_bid() is None or best_ask() is None or best_bid() < best_ask()

place("sell", 200, 10020); place("sell", 400, 10025); place("buy", 300, 10010); place("buy", 500, 10005)
print(best_bid(), best_ask(), invariant())
place("buy", 500)                      # market buy 500: predict the two trades
print(trades)
print(best_ask(), invariant())
# Your turn: 1) a limit buy at 10030 for 100 - which resting ask fills it and at what price (maker's price, not yours)?
# 2) write five asserts that pin the rules (price priority, time priority, partial fill, market order leaves nothing resting, invariant).
# 3) Boundary Question: a market order into an EMPTY book - what happens in your code, and what should happen?
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: the engine; because building the matcher is the only way to own price-time priority, and an AMM in FIN4 makes sense only against this; for the record (a hiring manager at a bank or exchange recognises this) and for FIN6. ONE IDEA: matching is a loop - while the incoming order can cross the best resting order, trade at the RESTING order's price, then rest what remains if it has a price. He reads the code first and explains `crosses`, the sort key, and why the maker's price is used (price improvement to the taker). Predict: 10010 10020 True; the market buy fills 200 @10020 and 300 @10025, leaving 100 @10025 on the ask; best_ask 10025 True. Task 1: fills 100 @10025 (the resting price), nothing rests. Task 2: he writes the asserts as a `def test_...()` block; run them. Task 3: today the market order silently leaves qty unfilled and returns - he decides (reject or report unfilled) and implements. Integer cents: say why once (0.1 + 0.2). HIS MACHINE: save fin2/orderbook.py with the tests, commit 'fin2: matching engine with price-time priority + tests', push. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: outputs, the five asserts passing, the commit.

Map the Canadian regulators: CSA/provincial regulators, CIRO, OSFI, the exchanges' own rules - and what each would care about in a tokenized security
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: post-trade and regulators; because 'tokenization will remove T+1 and the CCP' is the central claim he will evaluate in FIN5, and he cannot evaluate it without knowing what they do; for FIN3 and FIN5. ONE IDEA: after a match, a central counterparty steps between buyer and seller (novation), nets obligations and guarantees settlement with margin and a default fund; settlement moves the security and the cash on T+1 (Canada and the US moved from T+2 to T+1 on 27-28 May 2024). Regulators: securities are provincial - the CSA coordinates the 13 regulators (OSC, AMF, BCSC...); CIRO (2023, merged IIROC and MFDA) oversees investment dealers, mutual fund dealers and marketplace trading; OSFI supervises federally regulated banks and insurers (prudential); exchanges have listing and trading rules. He draws the trade timeline and the regulator map, and for a hypothetical tokenized TSX share says which body cares about what (CSA: is it a security, prospectus/exemptions; CIRO: the dealer/marketplace; CDS: settlement; OSFI if a bank issues/custodies). steps.title: Risk arithmetic: position size, expectancy, drawdown, ruin
objectives: Compute expectancy from win rate and average win/loss; compute position size from a fixed fractional risk rule; explain max drawdown
Show with numbers why a 50% loss needs a 100% gain, and why risk of ruin depends on bet size, not on being right
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: the arithmetic of risk; because every blow-up - a trader, a crypto fund, a DeFi protocol - is this arithmetic ignored, and a security analyst at a bank sits next to the risk function; for the journal and FIN6. ONE IDEA: outcomes are a distribution; what you control is size. Worked numbers he does: expectancy = p*avgWin - (1-p)*avgLoss (e.g. 0.4*300 - 0.6*150 = +30 per trade: a 40% hit rate can be positive); fixed-fractional sizing: risk 1% of 10,000 with a 5% stop -> position 2,000; drawdown arithmetic: -50% needs +100%, -20% needs +25%; gambler's ruin: a fair coin bet with 10% of capital each time vs 1% - he reasons about variance (optionally simulates it in Python in 10 lines - the editor is there). Say plainly: none of this says what to trade; it says how any trading plan is measured. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: his three computations correct and the -50/+100 explanation. Boundary Question: a backtest with 70% win rate over 20 trades - why that number means almost nothing (sample size; selection) - the same scepticism he applies to a vendor's security claim.

steps.title: Derivatives as mechanisms: forwards, futures, options, margin
objectives: Draw the payoff of a long forward, a long call and a short put at expiry; explain margin and a margin call
Explain why derivatives exist (hedging, price discovery) and where leverage turns them into the thing that fails first
steps.tutor_brief: WHAT/WHY/WHAT FOR: derivatives; because perpetual futures are most of crypto trading volume and liquidation cascades are FIN6's subject, and options language (strike, expiry, delta) is everywhere in structured products a bank sells; mechanisms only. ONE IDEA: a derivative's value is a function of something else; its payoff diagram IS the contract. He draws three payoffs (x = price at expiry, y = profit): long forward (a line through the forward price), long call (flat at -premium, then up from the strike), short put (flat at +premium, then down below the strike - the one that 'earns income until it does not'). Futures: standardised, exchange-traded, daily mark-to-market with margin; margin call = post more or be closed. Leverage: a 10x position loses everything on a 10% move - the mechanism of a liquidation; name 'perpetual swap' and 'funding rate' once as FIN4/6 vocabulary. EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: the three diagrams described correctly and the margin mechanism in his words. steps.starter:
# FIN2-C8 ON YOUR MACHINE: sec-lab/fin2/journal/trades.csv and sec-lab/fin2/journal/report.py
# trades.csv header:  date,instrument,side,qty,entry,exit,stop,thesis
# PAPER ONLY. Prices in decimal strings; convert with Decimal, never float.
import csv, sys
from decimal import Decimal
from pathlib import Path

def load(path):
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return list(csv.DictReader(f))

def pnl(t):
    sign = 1 if t["side"] == "buy" else -1
    return sign * (Decimal(t["exit"]) - Decimal(t["entry"])) * Decimal(t["qty"])

def main():
    trades = load(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "trades.csv")
    results = [pnl(t) for t in trades]
    wins = [r for r in results if r > 0]
    equity, peak, maxdd = Decimal(0), Decimal(0), Decimal(0)
    for r in results:
        equity += r
        peak = max(peak, equity)
        maxdd = max(maxdd, peak - equity)
    n = len(results)
    print(f"trades={n} hit_rate={len(wins)/n:.0%} total={sum(results)} expectancy={sum(results)/n:.2f} max_drawdown={maxdd}")
    # Your turn: 1) add risk per trade = |entry - stop| * qty and the R-multiple (pnl / risk) column; 2) print the equity curve as a list;
    # 3) refuse a row whose stop is on the wrong side of the entry (a buy with stop above entry) with a clear message.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
